![](images/79/79525b86cbbbc191f9a19ffa817fdaebeb0d1f6bd99eb97ce3f642a7fdf6033e.svg)

This equation is equivalent to the system

$$
\{\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}+{x}_{3}=2 \\ -{x}_{1}+{x}_{2}-{x}_{3}=-2 \\ -3{x}_{1}-2{x}_{3}=1\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we reduce the augmented matrix of the system to reduced row echelon form (RREF):

$$
\begin{aligned} & \,\,[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 1 & 2 \\ -1 & 1 & -1 & -2 \\ -3 & 0 & -2 & 1\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2} & :={R}_{2}+{R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 1 & 2 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 & 0 \\ -3 & 0 & -2 & 1\end{aligned}] & {R}_{3} & :={R}_{3}+3{R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 1 & 2 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 & 7\end{aligned}] & {R}_{1} & :={R}_{1}+(-1){R}_{3} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 & -5 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 & 7\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

From the reduced matrix above, we see that the pivot columns are the $1$st, $2$nd, and $3$rd columns. So,  $\mathcal{B}$ is indeed a basis of $\textrm{Span}\{\mathbf{a}_1,\mathbf{a}_2,\mathbf{a}_3,\mathbf{a}_4 \}.$
Also, the matrix tells us that $x_1=-5,$ $x_2=0,$ and $x_3=7,$ meaning that
![](images/c7/c732a274f27d98231f9a94dad40ff15f53e82f00b076ba46464ac640c2765703.svg)

Therefore, $x_1 + x_2 +  x_3 = (-5) + 0 + 7 = 2.$" :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id 17592186247170 :question/problem "Consider the vectors ${a}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}0 \\ -4\end{aligned}],{a}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}4 \\ 4\end{aligned}],$ and ${a}_{3}=[\begin{aligned}-4 \\ -4\end{aligned}].$ Find a basis of $S=\text{Span}\{{a}_{1},{a}_{2},{a}_{3}\}$  by inspection." :question/worked-solution "Remember that a basis of $S$ is a set of linearly independent vectors that spans $S.$

From the given vectors, we can see that ${a}_{3}$ is a linear combination of vectors ${a}_{1}$ and ${a}_{2}:$

$$
{a}_{3}=0\cdot {a}_{1}+(-1)\cdot {a}_{2}
$$

Consequently, the vector ${a}_{3}$ can be removed from $\text{Span}\{{a}_{1},{a}_{2},{a}_{3}\}$ without changing the span. So $S=\text{Span}\{{a}_{1},{a}_{2},{a}_{3}\}$ is spanned by just $\{{a}_{1},{a}_{2}\}.$ 

Lastly, note that ${a}_{1}$ and ${a}_{2}$ are linearly independent since they are not parallel. So the set $\{{a}_{1},{a}_{2}\}$ is a linearly independent set that spans $S.$

Therefore, a basis of $S$ is $\{{a}_{1},{a}_{2}\},$ that is to say,

$$
B=\{{{[\begin{aligned}0 \\ -4\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{{a}_{1}},{{[\begin{aligned}4 \\ 4\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{{a}_{2}}\}.

So, we start by creating a matrix whose columns are made up of our vectors, and then we reduce the matrix to row echelon form:

$$
\begin{aligned} & [\begin{aligned}3 & -2 & -1 \\ 0 & 0 & -2 \\ 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

In this case, our matrix is already in a row echelon form.

The pivot columns correspond to linearly independent vectors, while the non-pivot columns correspond to linearly dependent vectors that can be removed. Here, the $1$st and $3$rd columns are pivot columns, while the $2$nd column is a non-pivot column.

The $1$st and $3$rd columns from the original matrix are ${a}_{1}$ and ${a}_{3}.$ So, a basis of $S$ is $\{{a}_{1},{a}_{3}\},$ that is to say, 

$$
B=\{[\begin{aligned}3 \\ 0 \\ 0\end{aligned}],[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ -2 \\ 0\end{aligned}]\}.
$$" :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id 17592186316712 :answer-field/correct "answer-29b21dda-de01-5604-87d6-f584e72f6811" :answer-field/choices ["answer-e75b98ee-ddb1-5ceb-8b26-88ce2b2c42d9" "answer-682a6b44-ab7e-500b-bb7e-d04456824f16" "answer-29b21dda-de01-5604-87d6-f584e72f6811" "answer-a7beabae-c19b-5ab1-bf80-b342b52cb235" "answer-aaa02ece-075b-5a23-8ec8-b922ddb2aea1"] :db/ensure [:answer-field/validate]} {:db/id "answer-e75b98ee-ddb1-5ceb-8b26-88ce2b2c42d9" :answer/id #uuid "e75b98ee-ddb1-5ceb-8b26-88ce2b2c42d9" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "B=\{[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ -2 \\ 0\end{aligned}]\}" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-682a6b44-ab7e-500b-bb7e-d04456824f16" :answer/id #uuid "682a6b44-ab7e-500b-bb7e-d04456824f16" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "B=\{[\begin{aligned}-2 \\ 0 \\ 0\end{aligned}]\}" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-29b21dda-de01-5604-87d6-f584e72f6811" :answer/id #uuid "29b21dda-de01-5604-87d6-f584e72f6811" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "B=\{[\begin{aligned}3 \\ 0 \\ 0\end{aligned}],[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ -2 \\ 0\end{aligned}]\}" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-a7beabae-c19b-5ab1-bf80-b342b52cb235" :answer/id #uuid "a7beabae-c19b-5ab1-bf80-b342b52cb235" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "B=\{[\begin{aligned}3 \\ 0 \\ 0\end{aligned}],[\begin{aligned}1 \\ -2 \\ 0\end{aligned}],[\begin{aligned}-2 \\ 0 \\ 0\end{aligned}]\}" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-aaa02ece-075b-5a23-8ec8-b922ddb2aea1" :answer/id #uuid "aaa02ece-075b-5a23-8ec8-b922ddb2aea1" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "B=\{[\begin{aligned}3 \\ 0 \\ 0\end{aligned}]\}" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id 17592186345207 :question/problem "The vectors ${a}_{1},$ ${a}_{2},$ and ${a}_{3}$ are given below. Determine whether $B=\{{a}_{1},{a}_{2}\}$ is a basis of $\text{Span}\{{a}_{1},{a}_{2},{a}_{3}\}.$ If that is the case, find ${x}_{1}\cdot {x}_{2},$ where ${a}_{3}={x}_{1}{a}_{1}+{x}_{2}{a}_{2}.$

$$
{a}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1\end{aligned}],\,{a}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 2\end{aligned}],\,{a}_{3}=[\begin{aligned}-6 \\ -10\end{aligned}]
$$" :question/worked-solution "We want to determine if $B$ is indeed a basis of $\text{Span}\{{a}_{1},{a}_{2},{a}_{3}\}.$ So, we want to find ${x}_{1},{x}_{2}\in R$ such that 

$$
{x}_{1}{{[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{{a}_{1}}+{x}_{2}{{[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 2\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{{a}_{2}}={{[\begin{aligned}-6 \\ -10\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{{a}_{3}}.
$$

This equation is equivalent to the system

$$
\{\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}+{x}_{2}=-6 \\ {x}_{1}+2{x}_{2}=-10\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we reduce the augmented matrix of the system to reduced row echelon form (RREF):

$$
\begin{aligned} & \,\,[\begin{aligned}1 & 1 & -6 \\ 1 & 2 & -10\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2} & :={R}_{2}+(-1){R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & 1 & -6 \\ 0 & 1 & -4\end{aligned}] & {R}_{1} & :={R}_{1}+(-1){R}_{2} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & -2 \\ 0 & 1 & -4\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

From the RREF matrix above, we see that the pivot columns are the $1$st and $2$nd columns. So,  $B$ is indeed a basis of $\text{Span}\{{a}_{1},{a}_{2},{a}_{3}\}.$
Also, the matrix tells us that ${x}_{1}=-2$ and ${x}_{2}=-4,$ meaning that

$$
(-2)\cdot {{[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{{a}_{1}}+(-4)\cdot {{[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 2\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{{a}_{2}}={{[\begin{aligned}-6 \\ -10\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{{a}_{3}}.
$$

Therefore, ${x}_{1}\cdot {x}_{2}=(-2)\cdot (-4)=8.$" :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id 17592186344690 :answer-field/choices ["answer-8d2d9553-3fcc-5436-9ae5-e9313490ab61"] :db/ensure [:answer-field/validate]} {:db/id "answer-8d2d9553-3fcc-5436-9ae5-e9313490ab61" :answer/id #uuid "8d2d9553-3fcc-5436-9ae5-e9313490ab61" :answer/type :answer.type/text :answer/value "$\{{a}_{1},{a}_{2}\}$ is not a basis of $\text{Span}\{{a}_{1},{a}_{2},{a}_{3}\}$" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id 17592186120524 :question/problem "The vectors ${a}_{1},$ ${a}_{2},$ ${a}_{3},$ and ${a}_{4}$ are given below. Determine whether $B=\{{a}_{1},{a}_{2},{a}_{3}\}$ is a basis of $\text{Span}\{{a}_{1},{a}_{2},{a}_{3},{a}_{4}\}.$ If that is the case, find ${x}_{1}+{x}_{2}+{x}_{3},$ where ${a}_{4}={x}_{1}{a}_{1}+{x}_{2}{a}_{2}+{x}_{3}{a}_{3}.$

$$
{a}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ -2 \\ 5\end{aligned}],\,{a}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 3 \\ -5\end{aligned}],\,{a}_{3}=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ -2 \\ 6\end{aligned}],\,{a}_{4}=[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 2 \\ 2\end{aligned}]
$$" :question/worked-solution "We want to determine if $B$ is indeed a basis of $\text{Span}\{{a}_{1},{a}_{2},{a}_{3},{a}_{4}\}.$ So, we want to find ${x}_{1},{x}_{2},{x}_{3}\in R$ such that 

$$
{x}_{1}{{[\begin{aligned}1 \\ -2 \\ 5\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{{a}_{1}}+{x}_{2}{{[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 3 \\ -5\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{{a}_{2}}+{x}_{3}{{[\begin{aligned}1 \\ -2 \\ 6\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{{a}_{3}}={{[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 2 \\ 2\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{{a}_{4}}.
$$

This equation is equivalent to the system

$$
\{\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}-{x}_{2}+{x}_{3}=-1 \\ -2{x}_{1}+3{x}_{2}-2{x}_{3}=2 \\ 5{x}_{1}-5{x}_{2}+6{x}_{3}=2\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we reduce the augmented matrix of the system to reduced row echelon form (RREF):

$$
\begin{aligned} & \,\,[\begin{aligned}1 & -1 & 1 & -1 \\ -2 & 3 & -2 & 2 \\ 5 & -5 & 6 & 2\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2} & :={R}_{2}+2{R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & -1 & 1 & -1 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 & 0 \\ 5 & -5 & 6 & 2\end{aligned}] & {R}_{3} & :={R}_{3}+(-5){R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & -1 & 1 & -1 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 & 7\end{aligned}] & {R}_{1} & :={R}_{1}+(-1){R}_{3} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & -1 & 0 & -8 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 & 7\end{aligned}] & {R}_{1} & :={R}_{1}+{R}_{2} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 & -8 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 & 7\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

From the reduced matrix above, we see that the pivot columns are the $1$st, $2$nd, and $3$rd columns. So,  $B$ is indeed a basis of $\text{Span}\{{a}_{1},{a}_{2},{a}_{3},{a}_{4}\}.$
Also, the matrix tells us that ${x}_{1}=-8,$ ${x}_{2}=0,$ and ${x}_{3}=7,$ meaning that

$$
(-8)\cdot {{[\begin{aligned}1 \\ -2 \\ 5\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{{a}_{1}}+0\cdot {{[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 3 \\ -5\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{{a}_{2}}+7\cdot {{[\begin{aligned}1 \\ -2 \\ 6\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{{a}_{3}}={{[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 2 \\ 2\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{{a}_{4}}.
$$

Therefore, ${x}_{1}+{x}_{2}+{x}_{3}=-8+0+7=-1.$" :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id 17592186344612 :answer-field/choices ["answer-931fbf19-90fd-5095-9ed2-228296291e7d"] :db/ensure [:answer-field/validate]} {:db/id "answer-931fbf19-90fd-5095-9ed2-228296291e7d" :answer/id #uuid "931fbf19-90fd-5095-9ed2-228296291e7d" :answer/type :answer.type/text :answer/value "$\{{a}_{1},{a}_{2},{a}_{3}\}$ is not a basis of $\text{Span}\{{a}_{1},{a}_{2},{a}_{3},{a}_{4}\}$" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]}]

$$

$$

$$" :question/worked-solution "We want to determine if $B$ is indeed a basis of $\text{Span}{{a}_{1},{a}_{2},{a}_{3},{a}_{4}}.$ So, we want to find ${x}_{1},{x}_{2},{x}_{3}\in R$ such that 

$$
{x}_{1}{{[\begin{aligned}1 \\ -2 \\ 5\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{{a}_{1}}+{x}_{2}{{[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 3 \\ -5\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{{a}_{2}}+{x}_{3}{{[\begin{aligned}1 \\ -2 \\ 6\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{{a}_{3}}={{[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 2 \\ 2\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{{a}_{4}}.
$$

This equation is equivalent to the system

$$
{\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}-{x}_{2}+{x}_{3}=-1 \\ -2{x}_{1}+3{x}_{2}-2{x}_{3}=2 \\ 5{x}_{1}-5{x}_{2}+6{x}_{3}=2\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we reduce the augmented matrix of the system to reduced row echelon form (RREF):

$$
\begin{aligned} & \,\,[\begin{aligned}1 & -1 & 1 & -1 \\ -2 & 3 & -2 & 2 \\ 5 & -5 & 6 & 2\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2} & :={R}_{2}+2{R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & -1 & 1 & -1 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 & 0 \\ 5 & -5 & 6 & 2\end{aligned}] & {R}_{3} & :={R}_{3}+(-5){R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & -1 & 1 & -1 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 & 7\end{aligned}] & {R}_{1} & :={R}_{1}+(-1){R}_{3} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & -1 & 0 & -8 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 & 7\end{aligned}] & {R}_{1} & :={R}_{1}+{R}_{2} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 & -8 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 & 7\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

From the reduced matrix above, we see that the pivot columns are the $1$st, $2$nd, and $3$rd columns. So,  $B$ is indeed a basis of $\text{Span}{{a}_{1},{a}_{2},{a}_{3},{a}_{4}}.$
Also, the matrix tells us that ${x}_{1}=-8,$ ${x}_{2}=0,$ and ${x}_{3}=7,$ meaning that

$$
(-8)\cdot {{[\begin{aligned}1 \\ -2 \\ 5\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{{a}_{1}}+0\cdot {{[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 3 \\ -5\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{{a}_{2}}+7\cdot {{[\begin{aligned}1 \\ -2 \\ 6\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{{a}_{3}}={{[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 2 \\ 2\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{{a}_{4}}.
$$

1855} :activity/steps [{:db/id 17592186120688 :step/content {:db/id 17592186121040 :tutorial/content "A **basis** of a subspace $U$ (in $\mathbb{R}^n$) is a set of vectors in $\mathbb{R}^n$ that is linearly independent and spans $U.$

For example, consider the following subspace consisting of the span of three vectors:
![](images/aa/aaa76e82d8d54b305cfcfb0414f1fe7dd4d1c9d3ff932b4206a7b864922b394e.svg)

To find a basis of $U,$ we need to find a set of linearly independent vectors that spans $U.$

**Watch out!** The set
![](images/23/237305d1b82f44e0c365f721a33c35d8d983bd5facd4471d1885e8180ec7267e.svg)
is *not* a basis of $U.$ It's true that this set *spans* $U,$ but the vectors in this set are *not* linearly independent. In particular, the vector $\color{red}\mathbf{a}_3$ can be written as a linear combination of $\color{blue}\mathbf{a}_1$ and $\color{blue}\mathbf{a}_2$ as follows:

![](images/1d/1d0ff277adbace09315a1c0cd7c964eac41f5e2f080d0e32f888f379be435da0.svg)

To find a basis of $U = \textrm{Span} \{ {\color{blue}\mathbf{a}_1}, {\color{blue}\mathbf{a}_2}, {\color{red}\mathbf{a}_3} \},$ we can start with $\{ {\color{blue}\mathbf{a}_1}, {\color{blue}\mathbf{a}_2}, {\color{red}\mathbf{a}_3} \},$ but we need to remove any "redundant" vectors that can be written as a linear combination of other vectors in the set. In this case, we remove ${\color{red}\mathbf{a}_3}$ because it can be written as a linear combination of $\color{blue}\mathbf{a}_1$ and ${\color{blue}\mathbf{a}_2}.$

We are left with the set

![](images/79/79c529aa2fb5373ff9f8798300b1423ea63f90778bd4832ba1276f6af9c21f04.svg)

These two vectors are linearly independent (since they are not parallel), and removing a redundant vector does not change the span, so these vectors still span $U.$ That is to say,

$$
U = \textrm{Span} \{ {\color{blue}\mathbf{a}_1}, {\color{blue}\mathbf{a}_2}, {\color{red}\mathbf{a}_3} \} = \textrm{Span} \{ {\color{blue}\mathbf{a}_1}, {\color{blue}\mathbf{a}_2} \}.
$$

Therefore, the set $\mathcal{B} = \{ {\color{blue}\mathbf{a}_1}, {\color{blue}\mathbf{a}_2} \}$ is a basis of $U.$

**Note:** To see that the vectors $\{ {\color{blue}\mathbf{a}_1}, {\color{blue}\mathbf{a}_2} \}$ still span $U,$ first note that any vector $\mathbf{b} \in U$ can be written as a linear combination of the three original vectors:

$$
\mathbf{b} = x_1 {\color{blue}\mathbf{a}_1} + x_2 {\color{blue}\mathbf{a}_2} + x_3 {\color{red}\mathbf{a}_3}
$$

Since ${\color{red}\mathbf{a}_3} = -{\color{blue}\mathbf{a}_1}+3{\color{blue}\mathbf{a}_2},$ then we must have 

$$
\begin{aligned}b & ={x}_{1}{a}_{1}+{x}_{2}{a}_{2}+{x}_{3}(-{a}_{1}+3{a}_{2}) \\  & =({x}_{1}-{x}_{3}){a}_{1}+({x}_{2}+3{x}_{3}){a}_{2},\end{aligned}
$$

which shows that $\mathbf{b}$ can actually be written as a linear combination of only two vectors, ${\color{blue}\mathbf{a}_1}$ and ${\color{blue}\mathbf{a}_2}.$

Therefore, we can conclude that the set $\{ {\color{blue}\mathbf{a}_1}, {\color{blue}\mathbf{a}_2} \}$ spans the subspace $U = \textrm{Span} \{ {\color{blue}\mathbf{a}_1}, {\color{blue}\mathbf{a}_2}, {\color{red}\mathbf{a}_3} \}.$" :tutorial/id #uuid "4ff21f5d-5007-5b74-b135-bdb080fd5541" :tutorial/math-academy-id 3206 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} :step/id #uuid "be88e95e-9faa-5bfe-b721-4eda45231dc0" :step/math-academy-id 17504 :step/next {:db/id 17592186120689}} {:db/id 17592186120689 :step/content {:db/id 17592186119815 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186119626 :question/id #uuid "51c289e1-f118-5444-bf1d-c7e8262c549f" :question/math-academy-id "e-4816"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "f892805c-2c2c-5105-91ba-353aefe7b7f2" :knowledge-point/key-prerequisites [{:db/id 17592186050426}] :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186120517} {:db/id 17592186120518} {:db/id 17592186247170} {:db/id 17592186345006} {:db/id 17592186345007} {:db/id 17592186399713} {:db/id 17592186399720} {:db/id 17592186409635}] :knowledge-point/title "Finding a Basis of the Space Spanned by a Set of Vectors Using Inspection"} :step/id #uuid "1169ef7f-a019-5cfa-8ef6-1d2ff514f2f1" :step/math-academy-id 17505 :step/next {:db/id 17592186120752}} {:db/id 17592186120752 :step/content {:db/id 17592186121064 :tutorial/content "In the previous example, it was easy to see that one vector was a linear combination of the others. But what can we do when it's not so easy to tell? For example, consider the subspace

![](images/4c/4c12a6e56a6cc7cd72371c59f41b33d8876cf4b98aa40766f0e67ad1bc3a32f7.svg)

To find a subset of linearly independent vectors, we can put the vectors in a matrix and compute the reduced row echelon form:

$$
\begin{aligned} & [\begin{aligned}1 & -1 & -1 \\ -2 & 3 & 7\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2} & :={R}_{2}+2{R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & -1 & -1 \\ 0 & 1 & 5\end{aligned}] & {R}_{1} & :={R}_{1}+{R}_{2} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 4 \\ 0 & 1 & 5\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

The pivot columns correspond to linearly independent vectors, while the non-pivot columns correspond to linearly dependent (or redundant) vectors that can be removed. Here, the $1$st and $2$nd columns are pivot columns, while the $3$rd column is a non-pivot column.

**But watch out!** We need to pick the pivot columns from the *original matrix*, not from the reduced one.

Therefore, we can conclude that the set $\{ {\color{blue}\mathbf{a}_1}, {\color{blue}\mathbf{a}_2} \}$ spans the subspace $U = \textrm{Span} \{ {\color{blue}\mathbf{a}_1}, {\color{blue}\mathbf{a}_2}, {\color{red}\mathbf{a}_3} \}.$" :tutorial/id #uuid "4ff21f5d-5007-5b74-b135-bdb080fd5541" :tutorial/math-academy-id 3206 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} :step/id #uuid "be88e95e-9faa-5bfe-b721-4eda45231dc0" :step/math-academy-id 17504 :step/next {:db/id 17592186120689}} {:db/id 17592186121040 :tutorial/content "A **basis** of a subspace $U$ (in $\mathbb{R}^n$) is a set of vectors in $\mathbb{R}^n$ that is linearly independent and spans $U.$

For example, consider the following subspace consisting of the span of three vectors:
![](images/aa/aaa76e82d8d54b305cfcfb0414f1fe7dd4d1c9d3ff932b4206a7b864922b394e.svg)

To find a basis of $U,$ we need to find a set of linearly independent vectors that spans $U.$

**Watch out!** The set
![](images/23/237305d1b82f44e0c365f721a33c35d8d983bd5facd4471d1885e8180ec7267e.svg)
is *not* a basis of $U.$ It's true that this set *spans* $U,$ but the vectors in this set are *not* linearly independent. In particular, the vector $\color{red}\mathbf{a}_3$ can be written as a linear combination of $\color{blue}\mathbf{a}_1$ and $\color{blue}\mathbf{a}_2$ as follows:

![](images/1d/1d0ff277adbace09315a1c0cd7c964eac41f5e2f080d0e32f888f379be435da0.svg)

To find a basis of $U = \textrm{Span} \{ {\color{blue}\mathbf{a}_1}, {\color{blue}\mathbf{a}_2}, {\color{red}\mathbf{a}_3} \},$ we can start with $\{ {\color{blue}\mathbf{a}_1}, {\color{blue}\mathbf{a}_2}, {\color{red}\mathbf{a}_3} \},$ but we need to remove any "redundant" vectors that can be written as a linear combination of other vectors in the set. In this case, we remove ${\color{red}\mathbf{a}_3}$ because it can be written as a linear combination of $\color{blue}\mathbf{a}_1$ and ${\color{blue}\mathbf{a}_2}.$

We are left with the set

![](images/79/79c529aa2fb5373ff9f8798300b1423ea63f90778bd4832ba1276f6af9c21f04.svg)

These two vectors are linearly independent (since they are not parallel), and removing a redundant vector does not change the span, so these vectors still span $U.$ That is to say,

$$
U = \textrm{Span} \{ {\color{blue}\mathbf{a}_1}, {\color{blue}\mathbf{a}_2}, {\color{red}\mathbf{a}_3} \} = \textrm{Span} \{ {\color{blue}\mathbf{a}_1}, {\color{blue}\mathbf{a}_2} \}.
$$

Therefore, the set $\mathcal{B} = \{ {\color{blue}\mathbf{a}_1}, {\color{blue}\mathbf{a}_2} \}$ is a basis of $U.$

**Note:** To see that the vectors $\{ {\color{blue}\mathbf{a}_1}, {\color{blue}\mathbf{a}_2} \}$ still span $U,$ first note that any vector $\mathbf{b} \in U$ can be written as a linear combination of the three original vectors:

$$
\mathbf{b} = x_1 {\color{blue}\mathbf{a}_1} + x_2 {\color{blue}\mathbf{a}_2} + x_3 {\color{red}\mathbf{a}_3}
$$

Since ${\color{red}\mathbf{a}_3} = -{\color{blue}\mathbf{a}_1}+3{\color{blue}\mathbf{a}_2},$ then we must have 

$$
\begin{aligned}b & ={x}_{1}{a}_{1}+{x}_{2}{a}_{2}+{x}_{3}(-{a}_{1}+3{a}_{2}) \\  & =({x}_{1}-{x}_{3}){a}_{1}+({x}_{2}+3{x}_{3}){a}_{2},\end{aligned}
$$

which shows that $\mathbf{b}$ can actually be written as a linear combination of only two vectors, ${\color{blue}\mathbf{a}_1}$ and ${\color{blue}\mathbf{a}_2}.$

Therefore, we can conclude that the set $\{ {\color{blue}\mathbf{a}_1}, {\color{blue}\mathbf{a}_2} \}$ spans the subspace $U = \textrm{Span} \{ {\color{blue}\mathbf{a}_1}, {\color{blue}\mathbf{a}_2}, {\color{red}\mathbf{a}_3} \}.$" :tutorial/id #uuid "4ff21f5d-5007-5b74-b135-bdb080fd5541" :tutorial/math-academy-id 3206 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} {:db/id 17592186120689 :step/content {:db/id 17592186119815 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186119626 :question/id #uuid "51c289e1-f118-5444-bf1d-c7e8262c549f" :question/math-academy-id "e-4816"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "f892805c-2c2c-5105-91ba-353aefe7b7f2" :knowledge-point/key-prerequisites [{:db/id 17592186050426}] :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186120517} {:db/id 17592186120518} {:db/id 17592186247170} {:db/id 17592186345006} {:db/id 17592186345007} {:db/id 17592186399713} {:db/id 17592186399720} {:db/id 17592186409635}] :knowledge-point/title "Finding a Basis of the Space Spanned by a Set of Vectors Using Inspection"} :step/id #uuid "1169ef7f-a019-5cfa-8ef6-1d2ff514f2f1" :step/math-academy-id 17505 :step/next {:db/id 17592186120752}} {:db/id 17592186120752 :step/content {:db/id 17592186121064 :tutorial/content "In the previous example, it was easy to see that one vector was a linear combination of the others. This course is divided into three main categories: linear algebra, multivariable calculus, and probability & statistics. The linear algebra section covers crucial machine learning fundamentals such as matrices, vector spaces, diagonalization, projections, singular value decomposition, and regression, as well as dimensionality reduction techniques such as principal component analysis. The multivariable calculus section develops the tools needed for optimization and learning algorithms, including vector and matrix calculus.
